Family Health

Vulval itching at night: six possible causes and next steps

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Itching around the vaginal opening can feel particularly intrusive when you are trying to sleep. The cause may be an infection, a reaction to a product or a longer-term skin condition. Finding the right explanation matters because repeatedly applying the same cream can leave the actual problem untreated.

Why the itch can feel worse at night

People often call any itch in this area “vaginal itching”, but much of it affects the vulva, the external skin around the opening. Explaining whether the feeling is on the outside, inside or both helps the clinician decide what to examine. Notice whether the itch also involves the anus, pubic hair or skin elsewhere.

With fewer distractions at bedtime, an existing itch may become more noticeable. Heat, moisture or rubbing can also aggravate sensitive vulval skin. Some conditions, including pubic lice, commonly cause worse itching at night. Timing alone does not distinguish among them and does not mean the symptom is imagined.

The following six possibilities are a starting point for assessment, not a self-diagnosis checklist or a complete list of every cause. If the itch is disturbing sleep or repeatedly returning, it is reasonable to ask for help rather than wait for it to become severe.

1. Thrush

Candida is a yeast that can be present in the vagina without causing illness. Finding it in someone with no symptoms does not necessarily mean treatment is needed. When symptomatic thrush develops, it can cause vulval itching, soreness, discomfort with sex or urination and a change in discharge.

Because thrush is common, it is tempting to use an antifungal as soon as itching starts. The difficulty is that these symptoms can also occur with irritation or another infection. If the treatment does not help, adding more courses may delay the correct diagnosis.

A clinician may examine the area and test a sample of discharge, especially when symptoms are persistent, recurrent or unclear. Antifungal treatment can come in oral or vaginal forms, depending on the situation, and courses vary in length. Follow the instructions for the medicine recommended for you. Pregnancy, diabetes or reduced immunity can affect the assessment and treatment choice; tell the clinician or pharmacist before choosing a product.

2. Bacterial vaginosis

Bacterial vaginosis, or BV, is a common change in the vaginal bacterial balance. It can occur without symptoms. When symptoms appear, thin white or grey discharge and a fishy smell are more characteristic than itching. BV does not usually cause marked soreness or itch, so those symptoms may suggest another problem alongside it.

BV is associated with sexual activity, but it is not proof of an STI, poor cleanliness or anything about a partner’s fidelity. Its causes are more complex than a single germ in every case. Douching can disturb the vaginal environment and should not be used to try to clear the symptoms.

An examination and, where needed, a sample can help confirm the cause and rule out alternatives. Symptoms deserve advice even though BV sometimes settles spontaneously. Treatment generally uses prescribed antibiotics, including oral or vaginal options; thrush medicines do not treat BV.

3. Sexually transmitted or close-contact infections

Trichomoniasis is one infection that can cause genital itching, burning, redness, an unpleasant-smelling discharge or discomfort when peeing or having sex. Many people have no symptoms. Spotting or other unusual bleeding should also be assessed rather than attributed to a particular infection without a test.

A laboratory test can confirm trichomoniasis, and prescription oral medicine can treat it. Current partners also need treatment to reduce reinfection. Follow the clinic’s advice about avoiding sexual contact until treatment is complete and symptoms have resolved, and about follow-up testing. For sexually active women treated for trichomoniasis, CDC guidance recommends retesting at about three months.

Pubic lice are another possible explanation, especially when itching is worse at night. These tiny insects live in coarse body hair rather than inside the vagina. Lice or eggs attached to hairs may be visible, but they can be difficult to spot. A clinician or pharmacist can help confirm the finding and select an appropriate treatment.

Use a product intended for pubic lice exactly as directed. Head-lice products are not automatically interchangeable, and genital preparations must not be put near the eyes. Shaving alone will not remove an infestation. Clean recently used clothing, towels and bedding with the advised hot wash and drying cycle; items that cannot be washed may need dry cleaning or sealing in a bag for two weeks. Recent sexual contacts need advice and treatment as appropriate. Avoid close contact until the infestation has been treated. Return if live lice remain or symptoms persist, rather than repeatedly applying different pesticides.

4. Irritants and skin allergies

An itchy rash may follow direct irritation or an allergy to something touching the skin. Possible triggers include soap, bath bombs or bubble bath, laundry detergent, fragranced products, wet wipes and talcum powder. Spermicide, certain lubricants, latex condoms and topical medicines can also be relevant. Panty liners, tight clothing or synthetic underwear may contribute through ingredients, trapped moisture or rubbing.

A useful first step is to think about what changed before the itch began. Stop a suspected new cosmetic or cleansing product and simplify the routine. If symptoms might relate to a prescribed medicine, ask the prescriber how to proceed rather than stopping necessary treatment on your own.

Clean the outside gently, without a washcloth, sponge or scrub, and avoid washing inside the vagina. Fragranced or strongly cleansing products may worsen inflammation rather than solve it. A suitable soap substitute and other skin-care advice can be discussed with a clinician. Persistent dermatitis may need specific treatment or allergy assessment; removing one suspected trigger will not always settle it immediately.

5. Lichen planus

Lichen planus is an inflammatory condition that may affect skin, hair, nails and mucosal surfaces such as the mouth, vulva or vagina. Genital disease can cause soreness, erosions or ulcers and pale or white markings; elsewhere, itchy flat-topped bumps may appear pink, purple or darker than the surrounding skin. Appearance varies with the affected site and skin tone.

The immune system is involved, but a precise cause is often unclear. Certain infections, including hepatitis C, and some medicines have been associated with lichen planus or similar eruptions. Give the clinician a medication history, including anti-inflammatory medicines, and mention other recent health events. There are small reports of lichen planus after influenza vaccination, but their timing alone cannot establish the cause of a new itch. Do not stop a medicine or avoid recommended vaccination based on this symptom without an individual discussion.

Diagnosis usually begins with an examination, with a small skin sample sometimes needed when the appearance is unclear. Genital lichen planus often needs prescribed steroid treatment and specialist follow-up; other immune-modifying medicines may be considered when it is difficult to control. An antihistamine may sometimes help symptoms, but it does not treat the underlying inflammation. Tell the team about mouth symptoms, painful sex or changes suggesting scarring.

6. Lichen sclerosus

Lichen sclerosus is a long-term inflammatory skin condition, often affecting the vulva and skin around the anus. It is more common after menopause but can begin at other ages. Some people have few symptoms at first. Itchy pale or white patches, fragile skin, small cracks or blood blisters may develop, and soreness or bleeding can follow rubbing.

Over time, scarring can change the appearance or tightness of the tissues. Sex may become painful, and urine can sting affected skin. Anal discomfort or bleeding also needs assessment. These features are reasons for an examination; they are not a way to diagnose the condition from a description alone.

The cause is not fully understood. It occasionally occurs in relatives and is associated with some immune-related conditions, but this does not establish a simple inherited pattern. It should not be explained as an oestrogen deficiency or a general hormonal imbalance. It is not contagious.

A strong prescription steroid ointment is the usual treatment for controlling the inflammation, with a schedule and maintenance plan from the clinician. Injections, oral medicines or medicines used for persistent vulval pain are specialist options in selected circumstances, not interchangeable first treatments for an undiagnosed itch. Follow-up matters even when symptoms improve; report a new lump, thickened area or persistent ulcer.

When to arrange an assessment

Arrange an appointment if itching is severe, interrupts sleep, keeps returning or has not improved over a few days of gentle care. There is no need to endure it until a fixed deadline. Seek advice sooner for abnormal discharge, an unpleasant smell, sores, visible skin changes or pain.

Unexplained genital bleeding also needs assessment; if you are pregnant, contact your maternity service immediately about bleeding. During pregnancy, ask about itching and suitable medicines before self-treating. A previously familiar symptom can still have a different cause on a later occasion.

Tell the clinician when the itch began, how it varies through the day, what worsens it and which treatments you have tried. An examination, swab or other test may help distinguish infection from a skin condition. A biopsy is sometimes appropriate for a persistent or unclear lesion; it is not needed for every itch. If a treatment fails, follow-up can reconsider the diagnosis and the plan.

Reducing irritation and protecting sleep

Wear comfortable, loose clothing and breathable underwear, and avoid products or activities that increase rubbing or irritation. Use your hand for gentle external cleansing rather than scrubbing. Pat the area dry. Do not add deodorants or vaginal douches to cover an odour; a new odour is information to discuss with a clinician.

Avoid scratching as much as possible and keep nails short to limit skin damage. A cool external compress may ease discomfort briefly. If itching is keeping you awake, ask about appropriate relief instead of taking sedating medicines or applying several creams without advice. Symptom relief and treatment of the cause are separate parts of care.

Condoms lower the risk of many STIs, but they do not prevent every infection spread through skin contact and do not reliably prevent pubic lice. Keep up with screening appropriate to your circumstances and seek symptom-based care when needed; a routine cervical screening result does not diagnose the cause of vulval itching. Good skin care may reduce irritation, but it cannot prevent every infection or inflammatory condition.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The six causes require different assessments and treatments; nighttime timing is not a diagnosis.

Prescription treatment for inflammatory skin disease should follow an examination and a follow-up plan.

Infection care may involve partners and repeat testing as well as the initial medicine.

How BeMama can help

Write down one week of symptom timing, new products and attempted treatments if it helps, but arrange care sooner if symptoms are troublesome or concerning.

When to seek help

Seek assessment for persistent itch, genital bleeding, sores, skin changes or significant pain. Check medication choices during pregnancy and avoid applying general lice or itch products to sensitive tissues without instructions.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Itching felt around the vagina often comes from the external vulval skin.
  • Thrush is only one of several explanations.
  • Nighttime itch with pubic-hair findings may warrant a check for lice.
  • Lichen planus and lichen sclerosus need diagnosis-specific care.
  • Gentle skin care can help comfort while the cause is assessed.

Frequently asked questions

What symptoms can thrush cause?

Vulval itching and soreness, discomfort with urination or sex, and a change in discharge are possible. They overlap with other conditions, so persistent or uncertain symptoms may need examination and testing.

What are the usual symptoms of bacterial vaginosis?

Thin greyish or white discharge and a fishy smell are typical; some people have no symptoms. Marked itching is not usual and may have another explanation.

Does itching worse at night mean pubic lice?

No. Pubic lice can cause worse itching at night, but other conditions can also feel more noticeable then. Lice or eggs on body hair and an examination help identify an infestation.

Are lichen planus and lichen sclerosus the same condition?

No. Both can affect genital tissues and need medical assessment, but they have different patterns and care needs. Neither can be reliably identified from nighttime itching alone.

Can I prevent every episode with better washing?

No. Excessive washing, fragranced products and scrubbing can make symptoms worse. Gentle external care, comfortable clothing and avoiding known irritants may help, but do not prevent every cause.

When should I see a clinician?

Ask for help if itching is severe, disturbs sleep, persists over a few days or keeps returning. Seek advice sooner for bleeding, unusual discharge, sores, pain or visible changes, and discuss symptoms and medicines during pregnancy.

Should I keep repeating thrush treatment if it does not help?

No. Arrange a review so the cause can be checked. A skin condition, another infection or a reaction to the treatment itself may need a different approach.

Do condoms prevent pubic lice?

No, pubic lice can spread through close contact with affected hair and skin beyond the area covered by a condom. Condoms remain useful for reducing many other STI risks.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
